newsitem.title: USA: U.S. bank reform bill would add risks-OCC's Ludwig.
newsitem.headline: U.S. bank reform bill would add risks-OCC's Ludwig.

text.p: A top U.S. bank regulator warned Thursday that legislation before Congress to overhaul financial laws would jeopardize the safety and soundness of the banking system if enacted.
Comptroller of the Currency Eugene Ludwig told a House Commerce Committee subpanel that the bill would raise "significant safety and soundness issues" and "do more harm than good."
One provision of the bill would allow insurance regulators to prevent an insurance company that owned a bank from giving its bank financial support in time of crisis, Ludwig said.
"Under the bill, the insurance company may be able to walk away from a failed insured depository institution and shift the total liability to the taxpayers," he said.

In prepared testimony, Ludwig also criticized a provision in the bill that would allow a non-financial, commercial company to own a small bank without being subject to many rules imposed on financial companies that owned banks.

"There would be no assurance that the company had adequate capital to affiliate with an insured depository institution and no opportunity to evaluate the company's risk management tools and policies," he said.
Ludwig also said banks should be given more flexibility in the legislation to engage in new activities in direct subsidiaries instead of through affiliates of their holding companies.

The decision, he said, could have profound implications for the Community Reinvestment Act, which requires banks to make loans in poor and urban areas. Bank profits in subsidiaries would be subject to CRA, but profits from affiliates would not fall under the 1970s law.

"Over the long term, the requirement to conduct more profitable activities outside the bank is likely to cause a significant reduction in the relative portion of assets in the banking industry that are available to support the CRA," he said.
The Commerce Committee has until mid-September to complete its work on the bank reform bill, which was passed narrowly by the House Banking Committee last month.

Even if the committee approves a bill, the legislation faces an uncertain fate. Congress has been trying for more than a decade without success to reform the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act and overhaul financial regulations.
